author: Milton James
title: The Machinery of Aboriginal Disadvantage
text:
The Machinery of Aboriginal Disadvantage
I agree that divided responsibility can too easily become responsibility belonging to nobody. I agree that divided responsibility often results in costly duplication. But after more than thirty years working with disadvantaged young people, I have seen enough bureaucracy to know that rationalising services does not necessarily improve anyone’s life. More importantly, administrative efficiency is not the only principle by which good government should be judged.
Liberal democracy itself recognises this. We deliberately divide and disperse power, despite the inefficiencies this can create, because concentrated power carries risks of its own. Checks and balances inevitably produce some duplication, delay and friction. But that is the price we sometimes pay for preventing too much power being concentrated in too few hands. Efficiency favours concentration; accountability often requires its opposite.
This is where I part company with Pearson’s proposal. Removing layers of government bureaucracy may reduce duplication, but transferring greater responsibility to the Commonwealth while establishing more direct funding relationships with a smaller number of Indigenous organisations may also concentrate money, authority and decision-making power in fewer hands. We should therefore be careful that, in trying to solve the inefficiencies of fragmented bureaucracy, we do not simply replace several centres of power with a larger and more concentrated one.And we do not have to look very far to see why this is important.
Recent criminal proceedings involving people associated with the Cape York Land Council and Kalan Enterprises make that question particularly timely. Police allege that more than $400,000 was dishonestly obtained or used from the two organisations. The allegations are serious, but they remain allegations and will be determined by the courts. They should not be used to condemn indigenous organisations generally. They should, however, remind us of something rather elementary: Aboriginal-controlled organisations require checks and balances just as government departments, corporations and charities do.
The wider evidence gives us reason for concern. In 2021–22, the National Indigenous Australians Agency (NIAA) funded more than 1,000 external providers delivering approximately 1,500 Indigenous Advancement Strategy activities at a cost of $1.03 billion. The Australian National Audit Office subsequently found NIAA’s management of provider fraud and non-compliance only “partly effective”.
The problem, therefore, is not simply who controls the bureaucracy. It is the extraordinary amount of institutional machinery that has grown around Aboriginal disadvantage. Government departments, Indigenous corporations, land councils, institutes, consultants, academics, NGOs, administrators and service providers all occupy space between public expenditure and the disadvantaged person for whom that expenditure was intended.
Many people within these organisations do valuable work. But collectively they have also created an Aboriginal welfare and service industry. Like any industry, it can develop interests of its own. This presents an uncomfortable contradiction. The disadvantage of Aboriginal people generates the funding. Their needs generate programs. Their problems generate professional employment. Yet after decades of intervention, they can remain poor, unemployed and dependent.
Changing the racial or institutional identity of the people administering that system does not necessarily change this relationship. Moving power from a government bureaucracy to an Indigenous bureaucracy is still moving power between bureaucracies. We should instead be asking how much of that power and those resources can be moved further down—to individuals and families themselves.
As a social work practitioner, I have always regarded the purpose of intervention as ultimately making the practitioner less necessary—better still, out of a job. The same test should apply to Aboriginal policy. The measure of an employment service should not primarily be how much money it administers, how many staff it employs or how many clients appear on its books. The test should be how many people eventually cease needing it.
My experience with worker mobility provides one example. Instead of continually funding programs around an unemployed person, resources can be used to overcome the practical barriers preventing that person from entering the labour market: transport, accommodation, and off-site and on-site support and supervision during the transition to sustained employment. Once that transition occurs, something important takes place. The person’s income no longer comes from government but from wages. Economic power has begun to shift from institutions to individuals and families.That is also why I favour needs-based, non-discriminatory assistance. If a young Aborigine needs help entering the labour market, help them. If a disadvantaged white young person living in comparable circumstances needs the same assistance, help them too. The need should justify the assistance, and greater independence should be the objective.
One Nation has approached the problem differently, proposing to abolish NIAA, audit Indigenous expenditure and move assistance towards individual need rather than racial eligibility. Perhaps it is time to take that proposition seriously.
For more than half a century, Australian governments have progressively constructed a separate Aboriginal affairs machinery of departments, agencies, land councils, Indigenous corporations, community-controlled organisations, consultants and service providers. Its form has changed repeatedly, but the underlying direction has been towards treating Aboriginal disadvantage through an increasingly separate institutional system. Yet for many of the people at the bottom, the promised transformation has not occurred.
Perhaps Pearson’s proposal does not go far enough. Rather than deciding which Aboriginal bureaucracy should administer Aboriginal disadvantage, perhaps it is time to question the separate machinery itself.
Mainstreaming does not have to mean abandoning people who need assistance. Nor does it mean pretending that remote Aboriginal disadvantage is no different from disadvantage elsewhere. It means returning to a much simpler principle: Australians should receive assistance according to their needs, not their race, and wherever specialist assistance is genuinely required, it should have to justify itself by the results it produces.
On that question, One Nation may be closer to the mark.
After decades of Aboriginal policy, perhaps the most revealing measure of success is also the simplest: Not how much government spends. Not how many organisations it funds. But how many people no longer need either.
Milton James is a director of From the Bush Projects
